claim: CG8909 is the Drosophila LRP4 homologue.
source: We identified CG8909 as the fly LRP4 homologue (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2A), which is predicted to be a single-pass transmembrane protein whose domain organization resembles that of mammalian LRP4 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and domain organization comparison shown in figures.

claim: Drosophila LRP4 shares 38% identity with human LRP4 overall.
source: Drosophila LRP4 shares 38% identity with human LRP4 overall, 61% identity within the LDL-repeat containing extracellular portion, and 28% identity in the intracellular tail.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: Drosophila LRP4 shares 61% identity with human LRP4 within the LDL-repeat containing extracellular portion.
source: Drosophila LRP4 shares 38% identity with human LRP4 overall, 61% identity within the LDL-repeat containing extracellular portion, and 28% identity in the intracellular tail.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: Drosophila LRP4 shares 28% identity with human LRP4 in the intracellular tail.
source: Drosophila LRP4 shares 38% identity with human LRP4 overall, 61% identity within the LDL-repeat containing extracellular portion, and 28% identity in the intracellular tail.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: LRP4 is expressed throughout the adult Drosophila brain.
source: Consistent with previous expression data from whole-brain microarrays (Chintapalli et al., 2007), we determined that LRP4 was expressed throughout the adult brain using antibodies against the endogenous protein (Figure 1B–C) or an lrp4-GAL4 transgene that expresses GAL4 under the lrp4 promoter and visualized with either Syt-HA (Figure 1D) or an HA epitope-tagged LRP4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by antibody staining, GAL4 expression patterns, and previous microarray data.

claim: LRP4 is expressed in the antennal lobes.
source: All methods revealed similar patterns of expression in the antennal lobes (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E), optic lobes, and higher olfactory centers including the mushroom body and the lateral horn (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple visualization methods showing expression patterns.

claim: LRP4 is expressed in the optic lobes.
source: All methods revealed similar patterns of expression in the antennal lobes (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E), optic lobes, and higher olfactory centers including the mushroom body and the lateral horn (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple visualization methods showing expression patterns.

claim: LRP4 is expressed in the mushroom body.
source: All methods revealed similar patterns of expression in the antennal lobes (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E), optic lobes, and higher olfactory centers including the mushroom body and the lateral horn (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple visualization methods showing expression patterns.

claim: LRP4 is expressed in the lateral horn.
source: All methods revealed similar patterns of expression in the antennal lobes (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E), optic lobes, and higher olfactory centers including the mushroom body and the lateral horn (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple visualization methods showing expression patterns.

claim: LRP4 antibody staining is completely lost in lrp4 deletion mutants.
source: Antibody specificity was validated by the complete loss of signal in a deletion (see below) of the lrp4 coding region (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry showing absence of signal in mutants.

claim: LRP4 is enriched in the synaptic neuropil of the antennal lobe.
source: LRP4 was enriched in the synaptic neuropil of the antennal lobe (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry showing enrichment in neuropil regions.

claim: lrp4 is expressed in olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs).
source: These approaches revealed lrp4 expression in both olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) and projection neurons (PNs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by intersectional genetic strategies showing expression in ORNs.

claim: lrp4 is expressed in projection neurons (PNs).
source: These approaches revealed lrp4 expression in both olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) and projection neurons (PNs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by intersectional genetic strategies showing expression in PNs.

claim: LRP4 localizes to synaptic neuropil regions.
source: LRP4 localizes to synaptic neuropil regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy showing LRP4 localization in synaptic regions.

claim: LRP4 localizes either coincidentally with Bruchpilot or to the space adjacent to active zones.
source: Within individual expanded glomeruli of proExM-treated brains, LRP4 and Brp localized to similar regions (Figure 1E) and, when examined at high magnification, LRP4 localized either coincidentally with Brp (Figure 1F, arrowhead) or to the space adjacent to active zones (Figure 1F, arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy showing LRP4 localization relative to Bruchpilot.

claim: LRP4 localization is similar to that of known synaptic organizers.
source: This combination of active zone and periactive zone localization is similar to that of known synaptic organizers (Jepson et al., 2014; Li et al., 2007; Mosca et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published localization patterns of other synaptic organizers.

claim: 99.5% of lrp4-positive cells express the neuronal marker ELAV.
source: Nearly all lrp4-positive cells observed (99.5%) expressed the neuronal marker ELAV (Robinow and White, 1988) (Figure 1G), indicating that these cells were neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and ELAV.

claim: 0.4% of lrp4-positive cells express the glial marker Repo.
source: Few (0.4%) expressed the glial marker Repo (Xiong et al., 1994) (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and Repo.

claim: 59.1% of lrp4-positive cells express choline acetyltransferase (ChAT).
source: The majority of lrp4-positive cells (59.1%) also expressed choline acetyltransferase (ChAT; Figure 1I), a marker for cholinergic excitatory neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and ChAT.

claim: 22.4% of lrp4-positive cells express vGlut.
source: We also observed partial overlap between lrp4-positive neurons and vGlut (22.4%; Figure 1J), the vesicular transporter for glutamate.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and vGlut.

claim: 0.3% of lrp4-positive cells express GABA.
source: Interestingly, there was little overlap (0.3%) between lrp4 and GABA, the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in Drosophila (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and GABA.

claim: LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of excitatory cholinergic neurons.
source: Thus, LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of excitatory cholinergic neurons and a subset of glutamatergic neurons that may be excitatory or inhibitory, but is excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data with neurotransmitter markers.

claim: LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of glutamatergic neurons that may be excitatory or inhibitory.
source: Thus, LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of excitatory cholinergic neurons and a subset of glutamatergic neurons that may be excitatory or inhibitory, but is excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data with neurotransmitter markers.

claim: LRP4 is excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
source: Thus, LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of excitatory cholinergic neurons and a subset of glutamatergic neurons that may be excitatory or inhibitory, but is excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data showing minimal overlap with GABA.

claim: lrp4dalek mutants show a 31% reduction in the number of Brp-Short puncta in VA1v ORN axon terminals compared to control adults.
source: In ORN axon terminals projecting to the VA1v glomerulus in males (Figure 2B), lrp4dalek mutants (Figure 2C,H) showed a 31% reduction in the number of puncta for Brp-Short, an active zone marker, compared to control adults (Figure 2B,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in mutants versus controls.

claim: The reduction in Brp-Short puncta in lrp4dalek mutants is recapitulated by expressing RNAi against lrp4 only in ORNs.
source: This phenotype was recapitulated when we expressed any of four independent transgenic RNAi constructs against lrp4 only in ORNs (Figure 2D,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that LRP4 functions presynaptically in regulating active zone number.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing similar phenotypes to the null mutant.

claim: LRP4 functions presynaptically in regulating active zone number.
source: This phenotype was recapitulated when we expressed any of four independent transgenic RNAi constructs against lrp4 only in ORNs (Figure 2D,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that LRP4 functions presynaptically in regulating active zone number.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-autonomous RNAi experiments in presynaptic neurons.

claim: lrp4 loss-of-function has no effect on neurite volume in ORNs.
source: These changes were independent of glomerular volume: lrp4 loss-of-function had no effect on neurite volume (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of neurite volume showing no change.

claim: Loss of lrp4 decreases Dα7-EGFP puncta numbers by 29% in PN dendrites compared to controls.
source: Loss of lrp4 decreased Dα7-EGFP puncta numbers by 29% compared to controls (Figure 2F–G,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of postsynaptic receptor puncta.

claim: The postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor deficit in lrp4 mutants is independent of neurite volume.
source: This deficit was also independent of neurite volume (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), again demonstrating that lrp4 perturbation phenotypes did not result from decreased neuronal projection size.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification showing no change in neurite volume.

claim: LRP4 overexpression in ORNs increases the number of Brp-Short puncta by 30%.
source: LRP4 overexpression increased the number of Brp-Short puncta by 30% (Figure 2E,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2); this increase was also independent of neurite volume (Figure 2h and Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3) as the glomeruli remained the same size.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in overexpression conditions.

claim: The increase in Brp-Short puncta from LRP4 overexpression is independent of neurite volume.
source: LRP4 overexpression increased the number of Brp-Short puncta by 30% (Figure 2E,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2); this increase was also independent of neurite volume (Figure 2h and Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3) as the glomeruli remained the same size.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification showing no change in glomerular volume.

claim: There is a direct relationship between presynaptic LRP4 expression and synapse number in excitatory neurons.
source: Thus, there is a direct relationship between presynaptic LRP4 expression and synapse number in excitatory neurons: removing LRP4 reduces, while overexpressing LRP4 increases, synapse number.
evidence: The claim is supported by loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments showing opposite effects.

claim: lrp4dalek mutants show a 31% reduction in T-bar profiles per terminal in putative ORN terminals.
source: T-bar profiles were evident in both genotypes, but were reduced in number by 31% in mutant terminals (Figure 3C), which exactly matched the reduction observed by Brp-Short puncta measurements (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification of T-bar profiles.

claim: Terminal perimeter is slightly but significantly increased in lrp4dalek terminals.
source: Terminal perimeter was slightly but significantly increased in lrp4dalek terminals (Figure 3D), resulting in a 36% reduction in T-bar density when compared to control (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy measurements of terminal perimeter.

claim: lrp4dalek mutants show a 36% reduction in T-bar density compared to control.
source: Terminal perimeter was slightly but significantly increased in lrp4dalek terminals (Figure 3D), resulting in a 36% reduction in T-bar density when compared to control (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification of T-bar density.

claim: LRP4 is necessary for the proper number of synapses in putative ORN terminals of the antennal lobe.
source: These results are consistent with those observed via confocal microscopy, and demonstrate that LRP4 is necessary for the proper number of synapses in putative ORN terminals of the antennal lobe.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data confirming light microscopy findings.

claim: The majority of T-bars in lrp4 mutants display one or more morphological defects.
source: However, whereas irregular T-bars in control animals were rare (<5% of total T-bars), the majority of T-bars in lrp4 mutants displayed one or more defects (Figure 3L–Q), including immature T-bars that lacked tops (Figure 3L), detached T-bars (Figure 3M), misshapen T-bars of varying configurations and aggregations (Figure 3N–P), and multiple T-bars beyond those observed in control animals (Figure 3Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy showing various T-bar morphology defects.

claim: LRP4 is required for individual active zones to assume normal morphology, attach to the membrane, and have proper spacing.
source: Thus, in addition to controlling the number of synapses, LRP4 is also required for individual active zones to assume normal morphology, attach to the membrane, and have proper spacing.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy showing multiple types of T-bar defects.

claim: Loss of lrp4 in GABAergic inhibitory neurons does not affect synapse number.
source: When LRP4 function was impaired using the lrp4dalek mutant or RNAi in these neurons, synapse number was unaffected (Figure 4A–B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in inhibitory neurons.

claim: The reduction of synapse number under LRP4 loss-of-function conditions is specific for excitatory neurons.
source: Thus, the reduction of synapse number under LRP4 loss-of-function conditions appeared specific for excitatory neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing effects in excitatory versus inhibitory neurons.

claim: LRP4 overexpression in inhibitory neurons increases synapse number by 35%.
source: Interestingly, when LRP4 was overexpressed in inhibitory neurons, we observed a 35% increase in synapse number without an accompanying change in neurite volume, similar to what we observed for excitatory neurons (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in inhibitory neurons overexpressing LRP4.

claim: Inhibitory GABAergic neurons possess the downstream machinery necessary for LRP4 to function in adding synapses.
source: This suggests that, while inhibitory GABAergic neurons do not normally utilize LRP4 to regulate synapse number, they possess the downstream machinery necessary for LRP4 to function in adding synapses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the gain-of-function phenotype in inhibitory neurons.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons likely use distinct cell surface synaptic organizers that converge on common mechanisms for synapse addition.
source: As such, excitatory and inhibitory neurons likely use distinct cell surface synaptic organizers (LRP4 for excitatory neurons) that converge on common mechanisms for synapse addition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential requirement but shared competency for LRP4 function.

claim: Loss of lrp4 in excitatory projection neurons reduces synapse number in the lateral horn by 40%.
source: In lrp4 mutants, the number of excitatory lateral horn synapses was reduced by 40%, consistent with a role for LRP4 in synapse formation (Figure 5B–C,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in lateral horn projection neurons.

claim: PN perturbation of lrp4 using RNAi reduces synapse number in the lateral horn similarly to the loss-of-function allele.
source: PN perturbation of lrp4 using RNAi reduced synapse number similarly to the loss-of-function allele, demonstrating a presynaptic role for lrp4 in these neurons (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing similar phenotypes to the null mutant.

claim: Perturbation of lrp4 in Mz699-positive inhibitory projection neurons has no effect on the number of synapses.
source: Perturbation of lrp4 in Mz699-positive iPNs, however, had no effect on the number of synapses (Figure 5D–E,G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) despite a slight reduction in neurite volume in lrp4dalek mutants (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in inhibitory projection neurons.

claim: LRP4 overexpression in Mz699-positive neurons increases synapse number.
source: Despite a lack of a loss-of-function phenotype, we observed an increase in synapse number when we overexpressed LRP4-HA in Mz699-positive neurons (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in inhibitory projection neurons overexpressing LRP4.

claim: LRP4 has a general role in promoting excitatory synapse number.
source: Thus, the results of lrp4 perturbation on excitatory and inhibitory synapses in the lateral horn resembled those of the antennal lobe, suggesting a general role for LRP4 in promoting excitatory synapse number.
evidence: The claim is inferred from similar phenotypes observed in multiple brain regions.

claim: Flies expressing lrp4 RNAi in ORNs exhibit a near complete abrogation of attractive behavior to apple cider vinegar.
source: Flies bearing both transgenes (and thus, reduced lrp4 expression) exhibited a near complete abrogation of attractive behavior and were no longer able to distinguish the attractive apple cider vinegar from a water control (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay quantification.

claim: Presynaptic LRP4 in ORNs is necessary for normal olfactory attraction behavior.
source: Thus, presynaptic LRP4 in ORNs is necessary for normal olfactory attraction behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral defects following ORN-specific LRP4 knockdown.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of GABABR2 and lrp4 in ORNs markedly suppresses the behavioral phenotype associated with lrp4 knockdown alone.
source: Simultaneous knockdown of GABABR2 and lrp4, however, markedly suppressed the behavioral phenotype associated with lrp4 knockdown alone (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay showing rescue of the phenotype.

claim: Olfactory attraction behavior requires a proper level of net excitatory drive in the antennal lobe circuit.
source: These results suggest that olfactory attraction behavior requires a proper level of net excitatory drive in the antennal lobe circuit and that defects caused by weakened excitatory synapses can be compensated for by reducing inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral suppression by reducing inhibition.

claim: Loss of lrp4 results in improper axonal accumulations of Bruchpilot in larval transverse nerves.
source: However, in lrp4dalek mutants, Bruchpilot improperly accumulated in the transverse nerves (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry showing Bruchpilot accumulation in nerves.

claim: Loss of srpk79D results in improper axonal accumulations of Bruchpilot in larval transverse nerves.
source: This kind of accumulation is rarely observed in wild type, but is also most notably associated with loss of SRPK79D (Figure 7C), a conserved serine-arginine protein kinase that localizes to NMJ terminals and negatively regulates premature active zone assembly before Bruchpilot reaches the fly NMJ (Johnson et al., 2009; Nieratschker et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and published data on SRPK79D function.

claim: Brp accumulation in lrp4 and srpk79D mutants is not accompanied by focal accumulations of Synaptotagmin I.
source: In both lrp4 and srpk79D mutants, Brp accumulation was not accompanied by focal accumulations of Synaptotagmin I, indicating that axonal trafficking is not generally impaired (Figure 7A–C) (Gindhart et al., 1998; Johnson et al., 2009; Nieratschker et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry showing absence of Synaptotagmin I accumulation.

claim: Venus-SRPK79D largely colocalizes with Brp-Short in ORN terminals.
source: When expressed only in VA1v ORNs, venus-SRPK79D localized to axon terminals and overlapped with Brp-Short, demonstrating localization with and adjacent to CNS active zones (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy showing colocalization.

claim: LRP4-HA and venus-SRPK79D exhibit coincident and adjacent localization in ORNs.
source: In the ORNs of expanded individual glomeruli, LRP4-HA and venus-SRPK79D exhibited coincident and adjacent localization (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy showing spatial relationship.

claim: Loss of lrp4 reduces synaptic SRPK79D levels by approximately 50%.
source: We also examined this synaptic localization in lrp4dalek mutants: loss of lrp4 reduced synaptic SRPK79D levels by ~50% (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of venus-SRPK79D fluorescence in mutants.

claim: LRP4 is necessary for the proper localization and/or expression of SRPK79D.
source: These results demonstrate that LRP4 is necessary for the proper localization and / or expression of SRPK79D and suggest that SRPK79D might act downstream of LRP4 to regulate synapse number.
evidence: The claim is supported by reduced SRPK79D levels in lrp4 mutants.

claim: LRP4 and SRPK79D are close enough to interact as shown by proximity ligation assays.
source: However, in the presence of both transgenes and the appropriate probes (Figure 7J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D), we detected positive signal indicating that the proteins were close enough to interact.
evidence: The claim is supported by proximity ligation assay showing positive signal.

claim: Reducing srpk79D function presynaptically results in a 15% reduction in the number of Brp-Short puncta.
source: First, reducing srpk79D function presynaptically using an established RNAi (Johnson et al., 2009) expressed in VA1v ORNs resulted in a 15% reduction in the number of Brp-Short puncta compared to control (Figure 8A–B,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta following RNAi knockdown.

claim: SRPK79D is required for normal CNS synapse number.
source: Thus, SRPK79D is required for normal CNS synapse number.
evidence: The claim is supported by the reduction in synapse number following srpk79D knockdown.

claim: Concurrent removal of one copy each of lrp4 and srpk79D results in a significant reduction in Brp-Short puncta.
source: However, when one copy of each was concurrently removed, we observed a significant reduction in Brp-Short puncta (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing synergistic effects.

claim: LRP4 and SRPK79D function in the same genetic pathway.
source: This suggests that the two function in the same genetic pathway and may work together to ensure proper synapse number.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic interaction data.

claim: Presynaptic overexpression of SRPK79D partially suppresses the synaptic phenotype associated with the lrp4dalek mutation.
source: Presynaptic overexpression of SRPK79D in VA1v ORNs partially suppressed the synaptic phenotype associated with the lrp4dalek mutation, resulting in 92% of the normal number of synapses (Figure 8A,C–E), whereas overexpression of SRPK79D in a wild-type background had no effect (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in rescue experiments.

claim: LRP4 requires SRPK79D to mediate its overexpression phenotype.
source: When LRP4 was overexpressed concurrently with srpk79D RNAi, the phenotype resembled that of srpk79D RNAi alone (Figure 8E). This suggests that LRP4 requires SRPK79D to mediate its overexpression phenotype, likely by functioning through SRPK79D to increase the number of synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by epistasis experiments showing SRPK79D is required for LRP4 overexpression effects.

claim: LRP4 and SRPK79D closely interact presynaptically in the same genetic pathway to ensure the proper number of excitatory synapses.
source: Combined, these indicate that LRP4 and SRPK79D closely interact presynaptically in the same genetic pathway to ensure the proper number of excitatory synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple genetic interaction and epistasis experiments.

claim: Flies expressing srpk79D RNAi in all ORNs demonstrate a nearly complete abrogation of attraction behavior.
source: Flies expressing srpk79D RNAi in all ORNs demonstrated a nearly complete abrogation of attraction behavior (Figure 8F) that was indistinguishable from the lrp4 RNAi phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay quantification.

claim: SRPK79D overexpression partially suppresses the lrp4 loss-of-function behavioral phenotype.
source: Driving both SRPK79D overexpression and lrp4 RNAi in all ORNs, however, resulted in a partial suppression of the behavioral phenotype associated with lrp4 RNAi (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay showing rescue of the phenotype.

claim: SRPK79D is likely a key downstream effector of LRP4 in regulating synapse number and olfactory attraction behavior.
source: As the synaptic level of SRPK79D is positively regulated by LRP4 and SRPK79D overexpression suppresses the morphological and functional phenotypes associated with lrp4 loss-of-function, SRPK79D is likely a key downstream effector of LRP4 in regulating synapse number and thus, normal olfactory attraction behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic and functional relationships between LRP4 and SRPK79D.

claim: LRP4 is a synaptic protein whose expression may be preferential for excitatory neurons in the Drosophila CNS.
source: This study identifies LRP4 as a synaptic protein whose expression may be preferential for excitatory neurons in the Drosophila CNS (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis and colocalization with neurotransmitter markers.

claim: LRP4 functions presynaptically to regulate the number of active zones in presynaptic ORNs.
source: In the Drosophila CNS, LRP4 functions presynaptically to regulate the number of active zones in presynaptic ORNs (Figures 2–3) and acetylcholine receptor clusters in the PNs postsynaptic to those ORNs (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-autonomous manipulation experiments.

claim: LRP4 controls the morphology of individual active zones.
source: Moreover, LRP4 also controls the morphology of individual active zones: lrp4 mutant T-bars exhibit striking defects in patterning and biogenesis (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy showing T-bar morphology defects.

claim: LRP4 defects are specific for excitatory neurons.
source: These defects are specific for excitatory neurons, as inhibitory neuron synapses in the antennal lobe remain unaffected (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing effects in excitatory versus inhibitory neurons.

claim: LRP4 overexpression can increase synapse number cell autonomously in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Overexpression of LRP4, however, can increase synapse number cell autonomously in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Figures 2–4), suggesting that both share common mechanisms for synapse addition.
evidence: The claim is supported by gain-of-function experiments in both neuron types.

claim: The role for LRP4 extends to higher order olfactory neuropil in the lateral horn.
source: The role for LRP4 further extends to higher order olfactory neuropil in the lateral horn (Figure 5), suggesting that it may serve a general role in synaptic organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by similar phenotypes observed in multiple brain regions.

claim: Perturbation of LRP4 in excitatory ORNs abrogates olfactory attraction behavior.
source: Underscoring the functional importance of LRP4, its perturbation in excitatory ORNs abrogated olfactory attraction behavior (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays showing loss of attraction.

claim: A proper level of excitatory drive is important for functional circuit output.
source: The suppression of the behavioral phenotype by reducing presynaptic inhibition onto ORNs further suggests that a proper level of excitatory drive is important for functional circuit output.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral rescue by reducing inhibition.

claim: LRP4 likely functions through SRPK79D to mediate both morphological and behavioral effects.
source: To mediate both morphological and behavioral effects, LRP4 likely functions through SRPK79D, a conserved SR-protein kinase whose loss-of-function phenotypes resemble those of lrp4 (Figures 7–8), whose synaptic localization depends on LRP4 (Figure 7), who interacts genetically with and is physically in proximity to LRP4 (Figures 7–8), and whose overexpression suppresses the phenotypes associated with loss of lrp4 (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of genetic and molecular evidence.

claim: At the vertebrate neuromuscular junction, LRP4 forms a receptor complex with MuSK in muscle fibers to promote clustering of acetylcholine receptors in response to motoneuron-derived agrin.
source: At the vertebrate neuromuscular junction, one of these critical organizers is LRP4. There, it forms a receptor complex with MuSK in muscle fibers to promote clustering of acetylcholine receptors in response to motoneuron-derived agrin (Zhang et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2008; Weatherbee et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Muscle LRP4 can function as a retrograde signal with an unknown motoneuron receptor to regulate presynaptic differentiation.
source: Muscle LRP4 can also function as a retrograde signal with an unknown motoneuron receptor to regulate presynaptic differentiation (Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Motoneuron-derived LRP4 can regulate presynaptic differentiation, demonstrating a role for neuronal LRP4.
source: First, motoneuron-derived LRP4 can regulate presynaptic differentiation, demonstrating a role for neuronal LRP4 (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In the vertebrate central nervous system, agrin is not essential for synapse formation.
source: Second, in the vertebrate central nervous system (CNS), agrin is not essential for synapse formation (Daniels, 2012) though LRP4 can regulate synaptic plasticity, development, and cognitive function (Gomez et al., 2014; Pohlkamp et al., 2015), through functioning in astrocytes in some cases (Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: LRP4 can regulate synaptic plasticity, development, and cognitive function in the vertebrate CNS.
source: Second, in the vertebrate central nervous system (CNS), agrin is not essential for synapse formation (Daniels, 2012) though LRP4 can regulate synaptic plasticity, development, and cognitive function (Gomez et al., 2014; Pohlkamp et al., 2015), through functioning in astrocytes in some cases (Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Drosophila genome contains an LRP4 homologue, but no clear agrin or MuSK homologues.
source: In this vein, the Drosophila genome contains an LRP4 homologue, but no clear agrin or MuSK homologues (Adams et al., 2000), so any role for LRP4 there must be agrin-independent.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to genome annotation.

claim: Any role for LRP4 in Drosophila must be agrin-independent.
source: In this vein, the Drosophila genome contains an LRP4 homologue, but no clear agrin or MuSK homologues (Adams et al., 2000), so any role for LRP4 there must be agrin-independent.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of agrin and MuSK homologues in Drosophila.

claim: LRP4 functions largely through the conserved, presynaptic SR-protein kinase, SRPK79D.
source: LRP4 functions largely through the conserved, presynaptic SR-protein kinase, SRPK79D.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic and molecular interaction data.

claim: LRP4 and SRPK79D interact genetically and epistatically.
source: LRP4 and SRPK79D interact genetically and epistatically, as SRPK79D overexpression can suppress lrp4-related phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction and epistasis experiments.

claim: The role for LRP4 occurs preferentially in excitatory neurons.
source: Unexpectedly, this role for LRP4 occurs preferentially in excitatory neurons, as impairing lrp4 in inhibitory neurons has no effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential effects in excitatory versus inhibitory neurons.

claim: LRP4 may represent a conserved synaptic organizer that functions presynaptically, cell autonomously, and independently of agrin to coordinate synapse number and function.
source: Thus, LRP4 may represent a conserved synaptic organizer that functions presynaptically, cell autonomously, and independently of agrin to coordinate synapse number and function.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from all the experimental data presented.

claim: lrp4dalek mutants are viable with a slightly reduced body size.
source: lrp4dalek mutants were viable with a slightly reduced body size.
evidence: The claim is an observation from maintaining mutant stocks.

claim: Protein retention expansion microscopy achieves approximately 4-fold isotropic expansion of Drosophila CNS tissue.
source: Using protein-retention expansion microscopy (proExM), we obtained reliable, ~4 fold isotropic expansion of Drosophila CNS tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from expansion microscopy experiments.

claim: SRPK79D is a conserved serine-arginine protein kinase that localizes to NMJ terminals and negatively regulates premature active zone assembly before Bruchpilot reaches the fly NMJ.
source: This kind of accumulation is rarely observed in wild type, but is also most notably associated with loss of SRPK79D (Figure 7C), a conserved serine-arginine protein kinase that localizes to NMJ terminals and negatively regulates premature active zone assembly before Bruchpilot reaches the fly NMJ (Johnson et al., 2009; Nieratschker et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Distinct ALS and MG populations are seropositive for LRP4 autoantibodies.
source: Distinct ALS and MG populations are seropositive for LRP4 autoantibodies (Tsivgoulis et al., 2014; Tzartos et al., 2014) and double seronegative for Agrin or MuSK, suggesting that seropositivity is not a byproduct of generalized NMJ breakdown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Injection of LRP4 function-blocking antibodies into mice recapitulates myasthenia gravis.
source: Further, injection of LRP4 function-blocking antibodies into mice recapitulates MG (Shen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cognitive impairment occurs in a subset of ALS patients.
source: Beyond peripheral symptoms, cognitive impairment (besides that as frontotemporal dementia) also occurs in a subset of ALS patients (Ringholz et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The antennal lobe is the first olfactory processing center in the Drosophila CNS.
source: We further investigated LRP4 in the antennal lobe, the first olfactory processing center in the Drosophila CNS, which has emerged as a model circuit for studying sensory processing (Wilson, 2013) and whose synaptic organization was recently mapped at high resolution (Mosca and Luo, 2014).
evidence: The claim is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The antennal lobe has emerged as a model circuit for studying sensory processing.
source: We further investigated LRP4 in the antennal lobe, the first olfactory processing center in the Drosophila CNS, which has emerged as a model circuit for studying sensory processing (Wilson, 2013) and whose synaptic organization was recently mapped at high resolution (Mosca and Luo, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The synaptic organization of the antennal lobe was recently mapped at high resolution.
source: We further investigated LRP4 in the antennal lobe, the first olfactory processing center in the Drosophila CNS, which has emerged as a model circuit for studying sensory processing (Wilson, 2013) and whose synaptic organization was recently mapped at high resolution (Mosca and Luo, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Measurements from fluorescent synaptic marker methods are consistent with electron microscopy.
source: Further, measurements from these methods are consistent with our own electron microscopy (Mosca and Luo, 2014) as well as results from ultrastructural reconstructions of all synapses in individual glomeruli (Tobin et al., 2017) demonstrating their utility.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature showing consistency.

claim: Imbalances in excitation and inhibition lead to epileptic states.
source: Imbalances in excitation and inhibition lead to epileptic states (Badawy et al., 2012) and social dysfunction (Yizhar et al., 2011), and may also underlie many autism spectrum disorders (Mullins et al., 2016; Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Imbalances in excitation and inhibition lead to social dysfunction.
source: Imbalances in excitation and inhibition lead to epileptic states (Badawy et al., 2012) and social dysfunction (Yizhar et al., 2011), and may also underlie many autism spectrum disorders (Mullins et al., 2016; Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Imbalances in excitation and inhibition may underlie many autism spectrum disorders.
source: Imbalances in excitation and inhibition lead to epileptic states (Badawy et al., 2012) and social dysfunction (Yizhar et al., 2011), and may also underlie many autism spectrum disorders (Mullins et al., 2016; Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Postsynaptic factors like Neuroligin 2 organize inhibitory GABAergic synapses.
source: Postsynaptic factors like Neuroligin 2 (Graf et al., 2004), Gephyrin (Choii and Ko, 2015), and Slitrk3 (Takahashi et al., 2012) organize inhibitory GABAergic synapses while LRRTMs organize excitatory synapses (Siddiqui et al., 2013; de Wit et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LRRTMs organize excitatory synapses.
source: Postsynaptic factors like Neuroligin 2 (Graf et al., 2004), Gephyrin (Choii and Ko, 2015), and Slitrk3 (Takahashi et al., 2012) organize inhibitory GABAergic synapses while LRRTMs organize excitatory synapses (Siddiqui et al., 2013; de Wit et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Punctin/MADD-4 is a determinant of excitatory versus inhibitory neuromuscular synapses in C. elegans.
source: Recent work identified Punctin / MADD-4 as a determinant of excitatory versus inhibitory neuromuscular synapses in C. elegans, though as a secreted factor that functions via postsynaptic interaction (Maro et al., 2015; Pinan-Lucarré et al., 2014; Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Glypican4 can localize to excitatory presynaptic terminals and interact with LRRTM4.
source: Further, Glypican4 can localize to excitatory presynaptic terminals and interact with LRRTM4 (de Wit et al., 2013) but its synaptogenic activity is also provided by astrocytes (Allen et al., 2012) and thus is not neuronal specific.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the Drosophila olfactory system, glutamate can be inhibitory when its postsynaptic partners express glutamate-gated chloride channels.
source: In the Drosophila olfactory system, for example, glutamate can be inhibitory when its postsynaptic partners express glutamate-gated chloride channels (Liu and Wilson, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In the mouse CNS, LRP4 regulates synaptic physiology.
source: In the mouse CNS, LRP4 regulates synaptic physiology (Gomez et al., 2014; Pohlkamp et al., 2015), learning and memory, fear conditioning, and CA1 spine density (Gomez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the mouse CNS, LRP4 regulates learning and memory, fear conditioning, and CA1 spine density.
source: In the mouse CNS, LRP4 regulates synaptic physiology (Gomez et al., 2014; Pohlkamp et al., 2015), learning and memory, fear conditioning, and CA1 spine density (Gomez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CNS LRP4 most commonly associates with postsynaptic densities.
source: Though CNS LRP4 most commonly associates with postsynaptic densities (Tian et al., 2006), it also fractionates with synaptophysin-positive membranes (Gomez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CNS LRP4 also fractionates with synaptophysin-positive membranes.
source: Though CNS LRP4 most commonly associates with postsynaptic densities (Tian et al., 2006), it also fractionates with synaptophysin-positive membranes (Gomez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: This work is the first to demonstrate clear cell-autonomous presynaptic functions for LRP4.
source: While we cannot rule out an additional, perhaps concurrent, postsynaptic role, our work is the first to demonstrate clear cell-autonomous presynaptic functions for LRP4.
evidence: The claim is an assertion based on the novelty of the findings relative to published literature.

claim: The Agrin-independence of CNS LRP4 may be conserved across systems.
source: In Drosophila, the signal cannot be Agrin and in the mammalian CNS, Agrin is not essential for CNS synapse formation (Daniels, 2012). Thus, the Agrin-independence of CNS LRP4 may be conserved across systems.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of Agrin requirement in both systems.

claim: LRP4 promotes excitatory, but not inhibitory, synapse formation and function in the Drosophila CNS, which is consistent with reduced excitatory but normal inhibitory input in hippocampal CA1 neurons of lrp4 mutant mice.
source: Moreover, our finding that LRP4 promotes excitatory, but not inhibitory, synapse formation and function is consistent with reduced excitatory but normal inhibitory input in hippocampal CA1 neurons of lrp4 mutant mice (Gomez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published data from mouse studies.

claim: The three mammalian SRPK homologues are widely expressed in the mouse brain.
source: This kinase is evolutionarily conserved (Johnson et al., 2009) and the three mammalian homologues (Zhou and Fu, 2013) are widely expressed in the mouse brain (Lein et al., 2007), including in the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SRPKs regulate spliceosome assembly and gene expression from yeast to human.
source: From yeast to human, SRPKs regulate spliceosome assembly and gene expression (Zhou and Fu, 2013) but have not been studied in mammalian synapse formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SRPKs have not been studied in mammalian synapse formation.
source: From yeast to human, SRPKs regulate spliceosome assembly and gene expression (Zhou and Fu, 2013) but have not been studied in mammalian synapse formation.
evidence: The claim is an assertion about the state of the literature.
